To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the current system of specialist care for patients with rheumatologic diseases in Poland is not functioning properly.

(i) the current model of care for inflammatory rheumatic diseases is not effective, (ii) a reorganised model that includes early specialist diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis would be more efficient and effective, (iii) the model would require a significant investment in human resources (i.e. rheumatologists) and (iv) the model should be implemented in the next five years.
the current situation of rheumatology care is unsatisfactory and requires urgent changes.

the following issues: 1) the need to reorganise specialist outpatient care for patients with rheumatic diseases; 2) a proposed new model of specialist outpatient care for rheumatic diseases; and 3) the need for a new model of specialist rheumatologic care in Poland.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed model is a significant step forward towards the early diagnosis and treatment of inflammatory rheumatic diseases.
the current model of care in Poland does not allow for the timely diagnosis and treatment of inflammatory arthritis, and therefore it should be changed.
the proposed reorganisation of specialist rheumatological care in Poland is feasible and would significantly enhance the care provided to patients with suspected inflammatory arthritis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the reorganisation of specialist care for inflammatory rheumatic diseases in Poland would be a step forward in improving the health of Polish society.
the proposed reorganisation of rheumatology care should make it possible, for the vast majority of patients, to receive a diagnosis and initiate treatment within a period of 3 to 5 weeks.
the reorganised model should improve access to outpatient specialist care and reduce the time between the GP referral and diagnosis by a rheumatologists.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the proposed reorganisation of specialist rheumatological care in Poland should make it possible for the majority of patients with suspected arthritis to see a rheumatologist within 3–4 weeks of their referral by a general practitioner.
early diagnosis of rheumatic disease should be a priority for the Polish healthcare system.
